problem: Navigation services and prior instruction generators give turn-and-distance directions with street names, or rely on rule-based landmark selection. Earlier learned instruction generators only worked on simplified grid or indoor environments (Talk the Walk failed when more than one landmark was possible), or used panoramas without any human-navigation evaluation (Speaker-Follower). No large dataset existed of landmark instructions written purely from map data.
motivation: Humans process and remember landmark-based route instructions more easily than street-name/distance ones. Landmark instructions are useful when GPS is poor or distances and street names are imprecise, as for pedestrians, cyclists and public-transport users. OpenStreetMap is globally available and changes slowly, so a model that verbalizes salient, visible POIs directly from OSM could deploy widely. Unlike Street View, map data carries no transient features such as vehicles or construction.
key_idea: Encode an OSM route and its visible points of interest as a location- and rotation-invariant heterogeneous graph with binned-angle edge labels. Then treat landmark instruction generation as graph-to-text with a graph-attention Transformer, trained on the new crowd-sourced map2seq dataset whose instructions were validated by human navigation in Street View.
insight: Structure matters. A Transformer seq2seq fed a linearized rule-based instruction produces fluent, human-like text but gets directions wrong. On the partially-seen 200-instance human evaluation its SR is .160 and SNT .206, versus .540 / .676 for graph2text: explicit graph encoding of angles and route order is what makes the text navigable. Pretraining on 20k synthetic rule-based instructions teaches route sequentiality and angle semantics. This mostly helps generalization to unseen areas (unseen 200: SR .400→.429, landmarks 1.74→2.33, BLEU 14.07→15.64), while on partially seen routes SNT drops (.676→.537). Salience is learned implicitly: the model is given only geometric visibility, yet the landmark tags it chooses to mention (banks, pharmacies, parks, cinemas, coffee shops) closely match those in human references. Appendix analysis shows learned-model success drops as the number of turns grows, while human references stay stable.
method: Map discretization: Manhattan OSM extract from 2017, matching the Touchdown/StreetLearn panoramas; a street-segment node every 10 m. Routes are shortest paths of 35-45 nodes with at least 3 intersections, ending near a POI, and are verified to exist in the Street View graph.

POI visibility: for each street segment, POIs within a 30 m radius count as visible if the line to the POI (or to the nearest point of its polygon) does not cross a building polygon. No hand-crafted salience scores are used.

Route graph: typed nodes <street>, <poi>, <tag_key>, <tag_value> and <k_name_N> (name words). Route segments get positional tokens <1>, <2>, … and <last>; off-route segments get <neighbor>. Street–street and POI–street edges carry the angle relative to route direction, binned into 12 bins of 30° (first bin starts at 345°). This makes the graph location- and rotation-invariant.

Graph-to-text encoder: the input embedding is ReLU(W[type_emb || token_emb]). A 6-layer, 8-head graph attention encoder (GAT-style, attending only to first-order in-neighbors) uses relation-specific transformation matrices W^U_r per angle label, R-GCN style, plus skip connections.

Decoder: a standard 6-layer Transformer decoder attends over the final node representations, with a copy mechanism (pointer-generator) over node tokens. Embeddings are shared between node tokens and output tokens; d=256.

Pretraining (g2t+pretrain): the model is first trained on 20k rule-based instructions (POIs and intersections strung together with left/right) and then fine-tuned on the 5,667 human instructions. Early stopping uses token accuracy on the 605 dev instances.

Evaluation by human navigation: AMT workers follow the generated instructions in Street View (Touchdown panoramas). Success means stopping within 25 m of the goal. Metrics are SR (first try), SDTW, and SNT (success weighted by expected time / actual time, with expected time 1.3 s per route node).

setting.backbone: Graph-attention Transformer encoder + Transformer decoder with copy mechanism (6+6 layers, d=256, 8 heads; trained from scratch)
setting.model_size: 6 enc/6 dec layers, hidden 256 (parameter count not stated)
setting.training_data: map2seq train split: 5,667 crowd-sourced instructions (dataset total 7,672 human-validated instructions). g2t+pretrain is additionally pretrained on 20k synthetic rule-based instructions.
setting.observation: OpenStreetMap-derived route graph: route and neighboring street segments plus geometrically visible POIs with OSM tags and names, with binned angle edges. No visual input.
setting.action_space: N/A (instruction generation; outputs text). Downstream human navigators move in Street View via arrows.
setting.simulator: OpenStreetMap (input) + Google Street View / Touchdown static StreetLearn panoramas of lower Manhattan (human navigation evaluation)
setting.privileged: Full route and map, including POI locations, are the task input (speaker/generation setting). N/A for a navigation agent.

numbers_note: These are instruction-GENERATION results (speaker model). The navigation metrics (SR, SDTW, SNT) come from human AMT workers following the generated text in Street View, not from a navigation agent, so they are not comparable to later Map2Seq VLN-agent results. The paper prints SR/SDTW/SNT as fractions (e.g. .551); they are converted to 0-100 here. 'Landm' is the average number of landmark mentions per instruction, identified by token overlap with POI tag values. g2t+pretrain on the 200-instance subsets (same set as the graph2text/baseline rows): partially seen 'g2t+pretrain 18.81 52.5 2.44 .471 .540 .537'; unseen 'g2t+pretrain 15.64 50.3 2.33 .367 .429 .530'. Success-rate breakdowns by route length, intersections and turns appear only in appendix figures (Figs. 6-8).
results: On the 200-instance partially seen human evaluation, graph2text reaches SR .540 and SNT .676, far above the Transformer seq2seq baseline (SR .160 / SNT .206) and the rule-based baseline (SR .460 / SNT .455). The reference instructions reach SR .855 / SNT .878. On unseen routes the rule-based system has a higher raw SR (.525 vs .429 for g2t+pretrain) but lower SNT (.512 vs .530), because its landmark-dump instructions are slow to read. On the full 700-instance sets, g2t+pretrain reaches SNT .664 (partially seen) and .629 (unseen), versus .830 / .807 for human references. It produces about as many landmarks as humans on partially seen routes (2.41 vs 2.72).
limitations: Clear gap to human references (e.g. SR .473 vs .843 on unseen), and performance drops on geographically unseen areas with new landmark types and combinations.
Learned models' success decreases with more turns/intersections, whereas human references are stable. Baselines were only evaluated by humans on 200-instance subsets.
Restricted to lower Manhattan OSM/Street View. Visibility is purely geometric (30 m radius, building occlusion), and landmark counting uses token overlap.
compares_to: Transformer seq2seq with copy (rule-based → human instructions)
